title: Predictors of Athlete's Performance in Ultra-Endurance Mountain Races
authors: Belinchón-deMiguel P, Ruisoto P, Knechtle B, Nikolaidis PT, Herrera-Tapias B, Clemente-Suárez VJ
journal: International Journal of Environmental Research and Public Health
population: 448 finishers of ultra-endurance mountain races, grouped by race length (under 45 km, 45-90 km, over 90 km), by questionnaire.
findings: Higher performance was associated with better oral health status and higher accumulative altitude covered per week and higher positive accumulative altitude change per week in training.
In longer races, experience, a larger volume of training and better hydration/nutrition before the race were associated with better performance.
Athletes in races over 90 km had more experience and followed harder training schedules than those in shorter races.
For 45-90 km races, training intensity and volume were key predictors; for over 90 km, a larger fluid intake before the race was the single best predictor; for under 45 km, oral health status.
Psychological factors previously reported as predictors were inconsistent or failed to predict performance.
limitations: Questionnaire, finishers only (no DNF), no longest-run or back-to-back variable in the abstract, performance is finish time not finishing or injury.
implications: Supports volume and weekly climbing (not a single long run) as the performance predictors at 50-100 km; back vertical-gain in weekly targets for mountain races.
No evidence on the longest-run level, so no support for or against 180/240/270 min.

verification.notes: Re-fetched Crossref (IJERPH, 2021-01-22, Belinchón-deMiguel) and Europe PMC abstract (PMID 33499204). Findings match; added the under-45 km result. Wording 'accumulative altitude covered per week' kept close to the abstract.
